set.p: An interval of nearly a year is supposed to elapse between first and second acts, and an interval of two or three days between second and third acts.

div.head: Scene
div.stage: Scene.—Hall of a castle in the Highlands of Scotland. An oaken staircase on one side of the hall leads to the open door of a corridor. The hall is hung with banners and old Scottish weapons. Pointed windows. Through the high and spacious archway of door open at back, placed towards side, almost diagonally, are seen, first a narrow stretch of land, then a lake which it borders. The slopes of mountains descend beyond the lake on each side. Within the hall Ursula is at her wheel spinning. A group of hunters approach, and are heard singing the following chorus—

As the singing becomes audible, Ursula ceases to spin, and remains motionless. The hunters then appear, some of them bearing the slain stag upon their shoulders. They pass the archway repeating the chorus till their voices are lost in the distance. Sunset is visible through the archway.

sp.speaker: Urs.
sp.stage: [Rising and placing her wheel on one side.]

lg.l: Again the sun, like a spent warrior, drops
His flag of fire on the lake's breast, and dies.
The fifth night, yet no news. They must have met
Ere this—my brother, and his brave Macronalds,
And Murdoch, who leads on our mortal foes,
The fell Mackanes.
Roderick, are those returned
You sent for tidings to the pass?
Returned
From a vain quest.
Still vain! 'Tis now five days
Since the Mackanes hung on yon mountain's slope,
Scarce an hour's march hence. In a night my brother
Summoned his force to meet them—must have met them
In strife ere this.
Spoke I not truth to Angus?
I said, “Beware of the cat's stealthy windings.
Those posted on the slope are but decoys
Who seek to lure you onward to their land,
Where toil and hunger, fighting on their side,
Shall harm you more than steel.” Your brother reck'd not;
The lion's heart, with a child's brain to guide it,
Still urged him on; and now, perchance, ensnared,
He vainly struggles, while I, I—grown old—
A toothless mastiff dozing in the sun—
Must no more from the loosen'd leash bound forth
On my chief's foe, and shake him by the throat!
No; I'm no longer Roderick!
Nay, staunch heart!
The watchdog, like the bloodhound, has his use.
I know, did danger threat your chief's sole child,
My fair niece Lilian, you would find your tusks.
Thou say'st it, honoured dame. Methinks for her
Even these old gums would bite. Our Lady Lilian,
Our pride! nay more, our help! who, with the skill
In herbs and surgery she early gained,
Nursed me when wounded, tending all my needs
As she had been my daughter!
Ah! she loves
Better to staunch a wound than pay its due
To the bold hand that gave it.
Ay; she has lived
Till lately in a convent, where the sisters,
As is their pious trade, feed scrupulous souls
With saws of peace and mercy; wholesome fare
For mewed-up women, and sick, bedridden men.
Yes, there's a time for all things, for repentance
And mercy 'mong the rest. They're good, no doubt,
When the priest mumbles shrift, and one about
To quit this world must give up his old likings
To earn the next. Nay, nay, this mood will pass.
Our eaglet, 'scap'd her nun's cage, will by instinct
Learn the great swoop that fits Clanronald's brood!
Look, look! her barge makes land even now.

div.stage: [A boat is seen at back, gliding up the lake. The boat stops in centre of archway, and Lilian and Margery come on shore. The boatmen doff their bonnets to Lilian, and row on out of sight. Roderick advances to meet Lilian.

lg.l: Good Margery,
Take thou this mantle.

div.stage: [She gives it to her. Margery curtsies, and passes out at a side door.

lg.l: Daughter of Macronald,
Welcome! thrice welcome!
Thanks, thanks, Roderick.
What tidings of my father?
None.
None.
Strange!
You to the glen sent, and I now return
From where the witch's craig commands the lake.
Heaven guard my father and the clan of Ronald!
Oh, had I been his son, still to be found
At his right hand in danger!
A daughter, though she fight not, well may aid
Her father's cause. You are of age to marry.
The nephew of the Cameron sought your hand;
If you had wed him, you had gained your clan
A strong ally.
A crafty one, who sows
Strife 'twixt his neighbours that himself may thrive
Upon their loss. Well for us if the Camerons
Prove not our peril one day!
Shrewdly said.
There's young Macleod, the cousin of the chief,
Him you repulsed.
Macleod! He has flaxen hair
And a hand like a woman's; then he plays
The harp. The hand I take shall never finger
Harp-strings, but do the deeds that harp-strings echo.

div.stage: [The sunset has disappeared. A rather misty twilight comes on. A servant enters with a lighted torch, which he strikes into floor by mantel-piece: he then goes out.

lg.l: Thou hast a face to win men, and thou know'st it.
Ay, Roderick, ever since a child, I saw
That face reflected in your polished shield,
And to myself said, “Lilian's a beauty!
She's very much like dear Aunt Ursula.”

div.stage: [Throwing her arms round Ursula's neck.

lg.l: Yes, you know how to fool one. But say, Lilian,
If you refuse all strangers, why not wed
One of your clansmen? Malcolm long has wooed you.
My cousin? Oh, he's grave beyond his age.
I do not like a year without a spring,
Nor manhood without youth.
You scorned no less
Your distant kinsman Hector.
Oh, she scorns
Them all in turn. Yet Hector's handsome.
Fierce
And handsome—tiger-like. I want a man.
What fault has Duncan?
Duncan has red hair.
Is that a fault?
A grievous fault to have
The roof of his brain in conflagration, yet
Within no spark of light or fire to cause it.
Duncan's a simple fool.
Well, then, young David?
Oh, David has black hair.
You like not black,
Nor red, nor flaxen—nor the shades between?
Ah, Roderick! 'tis the wearer, not the hair,
That's hard to fancy. Give me, then, a man
Who has the love of song like young Macleod,
Yet knows war's trade like Hector; fresh with youth
Like David, yet in counsel sage as Malcolm;
With Duncan's faith, and yet without his folly;
And that particular shade of hair that suits me;
And then—
Well, then?
I'll look at the man twice
Ere I say, Go your way; but would he win
My heart, indeed, let him be brave, as is
My father, yet respect a noble foe;
And, if he vanquish, spare him.
Spare a foe!
Next to her hope of heaven a chieftain's daughter
Should love her clan; next to perdition, hate
Its enemies!
I hate all wrong, and all
Who work wrong while they work it.
While they work it.
No “whiles,” child! Hate's the cordial wine that warms
The heart; but “whiles” and “ifs” are the mere water
That mars the draught and thins the drinker's blood.
Give me hate neat! I like not drink diluted.
Nay, Roderick, well did Abbess Hilda teach
That we, who all offend, should mercy show
To those who share our taint.

div.stage: [Sits at table.

lg.l: The convent's prate
Where thou wast bred.
Think of your cause to loathe
The clan Mackane!
A husband's death I owe them;
And you a mother's! she my brother's wife.
Have you forgot the tale? Recall and muse on it.
In such a month as this, when such a twilight
As deepens now had fallen, your father absent
With all brave hearts that rallied to his war-cry,
These wolves his warrior eye had like a torch
Scared back into their woods, besieged our hold.
Your mother, then about to bear that name,
Lay helpless in her chamber, when the glare
Of flames (for with a belt of fire Mackane
Had girt our walls) laughed redly at her casement!
By Mary's grace, a royal force on march
Drove back the assailants; quenched the spreading flames!
But she, who shuddering in that chamber lay,
Hands clenched, lips locked in fear, her upturned gaze
Fixed on the reddening sky, with scarce a moan
Gave to our house a new life—Lilian, thine—
And breathed her own to heaven! Recall that tale!
What had it been to have known a mother!
It was not so to be. Before she passed,
Thou know'st she saw distinct the fatal shape
Of that fierce Graham whom your ancestor
In sudden quarrel slew; since when, the phantom
We know as Graham's wraith has still appeared
To tell our race of danger or of death!
I would you had not named him.
Why?
Because
But three nights since I saw him!
Saw him?
Ay,
As you have oft portrayed him; by my bed
He stood, or seemed to stand, with gaze intent,
And long black hair that like a half-rent veil
Disclosed the fearful secret of his brow,
Frowning and pallid! From his bosom gashed,
One hand drew down the plaid and bared to sight
His gory wound; the other bore his sword,
Which pointed back, as beckoning me to follow;
While o'er his death-struck aspect flitted slow
A smile of triumph which, having passed, the shape—
As though it lived but in the evil light
Of that strange smile—passed with it!
Nay!

div.stage: [The spectre of Graham's wraith appears dimly through the archway in the mist which has deepened, and which now dissolves and shows the light of the moon. The moonlight is soft and subdued. The spectre becomes gradually distinct, and in all respects resembles the description given of it in preceding dialogue.

lg.l: I saw it,
Plain as that wall, that shield, or yonder—

div.stage: [Turning to archway, she perceives the spectre, and stands arrested. Ursula and Roderick, to whom the spectre remains invisible, also rise.

lg.l: Lilian!
Has fancy
Raised to her o'erwrought sense, the thing she feared?
I know thee, phantom! If, dread shape, thy summons
Be unto me, fresh chapleted with hopes
And half-blown joys of youth, may heaven forgive
The victim's blemish, and accept her life!
If for those near unto my heart thou com'st,
Or other ill dost to our house portend,
Heaven's mercy shield us! To its will, not thine,
Spirit of vengeance, I commit myself!
See, see! the smile fades from his face, and with it
He fades!
Gone! all is air!
He was, and is not!

div.stage: [Faintly, and sinking on a chair.

lg.l: Courage! you looked on nought.
Imagination
Is wont to breed such shows.
And you saw nothing?
Nothing.
'Tis strange! most strange!
What sound was that?
Hark! hark! It comes again! It swells! The tumult
Of fight, the clash of arms, the clansman's war-cry!
There's no such sound.
I hear none.
You will hear.

div.stage: Hector appears at archway, followed by two armed Clansmen guarding Kenelm, and by two or three Retainers.

lg.l: See to that boy, my prisoner, straightway guard him.

div.stage: [Clansmen bear off Kenelm by side door. The Retainers remain in the hall.

lg.l: You, Hector? say, what tidings?
The Mackanes—
Near you, and poised to swoop upon your nest—
Are by your brother and our clan o'ertaken;
Almost within your hearing they contend.
I through the fight cut way to bear you warning.
You, Roderick, for the women's safety care;
For me, my place is in the field; farewell!

div.stage: [Rushes out.

sp.speaker: Rod.

lg.l: Follow him, you, and with what speed you may
Bring tidings of the fight!

sp.stage: [Retainers hurry out after Hector. Huntsmen and servants pass the archway, and follow them with torches.

lg.l: Let's hope the better fate; but for the worse
Be still prepared. A boat lies by the shore;
At once, then, cross the lake and 'scape your foes!
Heed him, and follow! Haste! my almost mother.
Farewell!
And you?
Macronald's child, when foes invade his hearth,
May die there, but not quit it!

div.stage: [She takes her stand upon the hearthstone.

lg.l: That's my place!
You are young, and, should they conquer, you brave death,
Or worse than death!
For death I am prepared;
And worse than death I can prevent.

div.stage: [She takes a dagger from old armour which surmounts mantel-piece, and conceals it beneath her plaid. The shouts of the combatants, mingled with the notes of the pipes, are now heard faintly in the distance.

lg.l: Hist! Now
You catch the shout!
Strike home, brave Angus! would
I could strike with you!

div.stage: [The shouts and notes of the pipes, though still distant, become more distinct. At length the cry, “Craig Eagalach!” “Craig Eagalach!” is remotely heard.

lg.l: 'Twas a single war-cry.
Whose? Again!

div.stage: [The cry, “Craig Eagalach!” “Craig Eagalach!” becomes still more distinct.

lg.l: It is but one shout, and that shout our own!
“Craig Eagalach!”—the Rock of Terror—yes,
The fight is o'er.
Your father comes a victor!

div.stage: [Triumphant music from the pipes of the Clanronald is now heard near. Suddenly the notes of triumph are exchanged for low wailing music.

lg.l: Why sink those notes of triumph to a wail?
They come! they come!

div.stage: Enter, preceded by servants with torches and others, the pipers and standard-bearer of the Macronalds, the latter bearing a flag with the crest, device of a castle, surmounted by a hand grasping a sword, and having above the motto, “My hope is constant in thee.” They are followed by Malcolm, Hector, Torquil, and many other of the Macronalds. Malcolm, Hector, Torquil, and one or two others, as kinsmen of the chief, wear each an eagle's feather in his bonnet. The general body wear in their bonnets heath the badge of the Macronalds. Some carry double-edged swords, targets, and daggers, others the same (targets excepted) with the addition of bows and arrows. The low wail from bagpipes continues till all have entered.

lg.l: Speak, Malcolm, Torquil, speak!
Victory is yours we know, but at what cost?

div.stage: [Hector retires, and goes out at side door. Musicians retire at back, and await the body of Angus.

lg.l: What woe these sounds lament too soon, too soon
Shall grieve your ears. But take our whole brief story.—
As you guessed, Roderick, the foemen's line,
Seen on yon hills, was meant but to decoy.
The scanty band retreating, lured us on
Into their hostile land! At length young David—
Hector's dear foster-brother—with the ardour
Of nineteen summers, darted from our ranks
And neared the foe, who then, with sudden onset,
Closed round and seized him! Not his youth nor courage
Touched their fierce hearts. A dozen daggers gleamed,
And in the stripling's bosom found their sheaths!
Heaven forget me, if ever I forget
That white and beardless face!
O wolves, not men!
Still hold you firm; this grief a greater heralds,
That bids all listeners stand unbonneted
For a dead king on his bier! O, ask not words;
Think what our clan holds its best strength—its pride—
Even that we lack!
Cease, raven! Say thou speak'st not
Of Angus, of our chief?
Not of my father?
Cousin, too true, too true, your father's dead!
Dead, say you? Then of his fate, not of mine,
The spectre warned me. Father!

div.stage: [Sits absorbed in grief.

lg.l: Say, how fell he?
With feet by vengeance winged, on David's murderers
We rushed, and at the sword's edge forced confession
That their chief strength was marching on our home.
Swift we pursued, and where the misty moon
Showed our old tower, o'ertook them, when a shaft—
A cursed shaft—struck noble Angus down!
My chief! And I live on!
Farewell, my brother!
Thou diedst as should my brother!
We avenged him;
For like a crag, that, loosened from its height,
Rings down the echoing slope, we burst upon them!
Before the shock they fled. To us returned,
Falls the sad task to tell you of that loss
Which we share with you.
Nephew, thanks! For me,
I'll to my chamber. Lilian!

div.stage: [Lilian rises. Roderick takes a torch from an attendant, and ushers Ursula and Lilian, whom Ursula supports, to the foot of the staircase leading to corridor.

lg.l: May all saints
Have you in keeping! Upon me unworthy
Now lights the state of chief; command me ever.
Cousin and aunt, good night!

div.stage: [Malcolm and Clansmen bow with deep reverence, while Ursula, preceded by Roderick with torch, and followed by Lilian, begin to ascend staircase.
Re-enter, from side door, Hector, dragging Kenelm, who wears the Mackane plaid and a sprig of holly in his cap.

lg.l: A prize! a prize!
My prize!
What slip is this,
That in our sight doth bear the holly badge
Of the Mackanes?

div.stage: [Ursula, preceded by Roderick, disappears in corridor. Lilian, arrested by the sight of Kenelm and by the tumult, remains on staircase.

lg.l: While through their land we pressed,
I, smit with thirst, entering a cottar's house,
Chanced on this boy, charge of a crone with whom,
For more concealment while his kin were absent,
His father placed him! But his look and garb
Spoke the lad's rank. I bore him off; but when
I and my fellows following gained our rear,
The fight was hottest. Natheless, through the strife
We held the boy in guard, and hither brought him.
'Tis Murdoch's son, chief of the clan Mackane:
He has confessed it.
Murdoch's son!
Thy name?

div.stage: [Kenelm shrinks back.

lg.l: He weeps. His father has caused tears enough.
Quickly, thy name?

div.stage: [Kenelm is silent.

lg.l: He fears or shames to speak it.
Thou liest! I am the son of Murdoch, chief
Of the Mackanes. 'Tis thou, not I, would fear,
Dog of Macronald, were my father by!
There spoke his father's son. Malcolm, remember
Young David murdered, my loved foster-brother,
Whose fresh wounds cry, “Revenge!” Let that revenge
Reach all Mackanes through him!

div.stage: [Pointing to Kenelm.

lg.l: Ay, son for son!
And blood for blood!
'Tis just!
Ye say so?
All!

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.stage: [Who has descended staircase, and advanced to the front.]

lg.l: Malcolm, what horror's this?
Thou here? retire!
This is no place for women.
Yes; where'er
The helpless cry for mercy, and man heeds not,
There is the place for women!
Did his tribe
Show our young David mercy?
No; he fell
A living target pierced with daggers! Cowards!
A score against a boy!
He dies!
He dies!
Can pity for my fate flow in thy veins?
Wouldst thou, an orphan, spare their ruthless seed
Who made thee such? Your father, girl, had crushed it.

sp.speaker: Lil.

lg.l: Thou dost defame him, Malcolm; and his blood,
Which flows direct in me as doth a stream
From a hid spring, doth tell thee thou defam'st him!

sp.stage: [She seizes Kenelm's hand. Clansmen on each side advance to obstruct her passage.

lg.l: My father, didst thou say? With him a man,
Armed to the teeth, ran danger; but a woman
And child were safe, being helpless.

sp.stage: [These words produce some impression on all except Hector.

lg.l: So with you;
So with you all.
Macronalds, hear your sister!
Fall ye to doubt? Lady, our chief has spoken.

div.stage: [He advances to seize Kenelm.

lg.l: Back! I am daughter of your dead chief Angus!
Command him back!

div.stage: [To Malcolm. Hector turns to Malcolm as for orders.

lg.l: Thou know'st my will. Retire,
Let go that hand.

sp.speaker: Lil.

lg.l: Not till some savage grasp
Wrench it from mine! There's no such here!
See, Malcolm—
See all—the banner of our race! Who looks
Upon these folds, nor feels a clansman's pride?
These folds, that, ever first in danger's track,
Waved heroes on! If by this deed ye stain
Your glorious flag, no more wear swords, but henceforth
Whet knives for shambles. I, for one, abjure
Macronald's name, and at my shrinking feet
Cast your loathed colours! Shall I? Speak?

sp.stage: [Seeing Roderick, who descends staircase with torch.

lg.l: Ah, Roderick!
Thou art a soldier. Take and shield this boy!

div.stage: [She gives Kenelm to Roderick and confronts Clansmen.

lg.l: A true Macronald!

div.stage: [Torquil and most of the Clansmen, but not Hector, signify assent, exclaiming, 'Tis Angus' daughter!

sp.speaker: Mal.

lg.l: Yes; her father's soul
Looks from her eyes!
Brothers, I may not spurn
A prayer so urged; the first prayer from the lips
Of Angus' child.
Doubt not we'll take revenge,
Signal, it may be nobler, for slain David.
Cousin, you have prevailed, the boy shall live,
But on these terms, or else he forfeits mercy,
That he no longer bears his people's name,

sp.stage: [A movement of indignation from Kenelm, which Lilian represses, and again takes his hand.

lg.l: Who shall not deem he lives; and that he rest,
Guarded within our power, so to be dealt with
By us as we by them. Thus much we grant
Your father's child.

sp.stage: [A wail of the pipes is heard from musicians at back.

lg.l: List! from the field they bear
His corse, the clay that once was Angus!

div.stage: [The wail is renewed. Roderick takes flag from Lilian. A friar advances by torchlight through archway at the head of a few clanspeople and domestics, including women and children of both sexes, who precede and surround the body of Angus. The group divide in front, and discover the body of Angus on a bier, the arms folded on the breast, the hands closed on a sword. The wail continues. All Clansmen uncover and bend in reverence.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.stage: [Advancing in solemn grief to the body and kneeling, her arm round Kenelm, who also uncovers and bends.]

lg.l: Father!

div.head: Scene
div.stage: Scene.—The Convent of St Catherine. An apartment overlooking at back, through open window, a terrace practicable, and garden doors on each side.

lg.l: Surely the hand of imp or fay has ravell'd
The skeins here, red, gold, blue; one tangled knot!
Did you say blue next? was it blue or gold?
You have not heard me, madam! Gold or blue?
Oh, either.
Gold; then blue.
There's gold, then.
Yes,
'Tis true—that which I told you—all is stir
And preparation. The young knight departs—
Madam, there's blue.
That he departs at all
Is due to you who healed him.
Margery,
You've said that oft.
Well, I shall scarcely miss
The good knight or his followers. All kind powers
Be praised, we quit this convent! Not a word,
Or even a look, allowed 'twixt us Macronalds
And those who serve Sir Oscar! True, they're French,
And, had we met, we scarce by words had guessed
Each other's thoughts. But then one's eyes can speak,
Though one's tongue fail.
Thy tongue, dear Margery,
Will scarce break down. I love to hear thee talk;
But now my task needs pains, and I must fix
My thoughts on it. Leave me, good Margery.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.stage: [Laying down work-bag, and glancing at Lilian's work.]

lg.l: You must work hard to end it ere 'tis Lammas.

div.stage: [Margery goes out by one of the side doors.

lg.l: To-day! He goes at noon—an hour and all
Will be as though it had not been. Not so;
Things we call past live on in their effects.

div.stage: Enter Roderick and Kenelm from garden. Kenelm wears no plaid or tartan of any kind, nor badge in his bonnet (which is a different one, as should be seen, from that of 1st Act), but a blue scarf. He is nearly a year older than in 1st Act.

sp.speaker: Ken.
sp.stage: [Who carries a foil rebated at the point.]

lg.l: Now, Roderick, to't again; up with thy staff!

div.stage: [Menacing him in sport with foil

lg.l: Give breathing-time; remember that my joints
Are rusty. Now then!

sp.speaker: Ken.
sp.stage: [Who, attacking, is parried by Roderick's staff.]

lg.l: By St David, thou
Hast eye and arm yet! What! thy joints want oil?
They're lithe as mine. Again!

sp.stage: [Kenelm again attacks, and is again parried.]

lg.l: Once more; have at thee!

div.stage: [He again attacks, and this time touches Roderick with foil.

lg.l: So,
Well planted! there you hit.
You let me do it.
But I am now fifteen. Come three years more,
I'll hit without your letting.
Whipster!

div.stage: [Laughs, and pats him on the head.

lg.l: Roderick!
I came for your commands. Do you still propose
To quit St Catherine's and your friend the abbess
So soon—to-morrow?
Yes; my cousin Malcolm
Sends, as you know, to urge my swift return.
'Tis thought the Camerons will soon break forth
In open strife.
Ay, now their chief unmasks
And shows a threatening front, both to our clan
And the Mackanes.
Did I not tell thee once
'Twas Cameron's art to thrive on other's loss?
As the wolf bears the prey from two spent lions.
Does Cameron threat my clan?
Not less than ours.
'Tis fixed, then; at what hour do you set forth,
To-morrow?

div.stage: [To Lilian.

sp.speaker: Lil.

lg.l: At an hour past dawn. Sit, Roderick.

sp.stage: [Roderick sits. Lilian aside, falling into reverie.

lg.l: He goes at noon. Were his brief words last night
Meant for a farewell? Shall we meet no more?

sp.speaker: Rod.

lg.l: I' faith, I shall be glad to see once more
Our castle walls.

sp.stage: [In a louder tone, observing that she does not reply.]

lg.l: I say these few weeks spent
'Neath Abbess Hilda's roof will stay my hunger
For convent life.
To me they have seemed brief.
You know that I was bred here, and the abbess
Was loved of my aunt Ursula.
A lady,
Most mourned and honoured, who too early joined
Your father in the grave.
Ay, aunt and father
Lost in one year. This month it counts a year
Since my brave father fell. Then Ursula,
To others stern, to me most gentle, followed.
Thus pass the friends of old; and new friends! They, too,
Come but to vanish!

div.stage: [Again in reverie.

lg.l: Dost thou say the Cameron
Threatens my father. Hence, toy!
Vain to learn
The sword's use, if I draw it not for him!
Wouldst thou be safe, forget him.
At that price
I'd not be safe. Mark, Roderick; dog my steps
And mesh me as you will, I'll some day 'scape,
For I will see my father.
Peace! such words
Might risk your life. Those in your lady's train
Assigned to guard you have quick eyes and ears.
Would I were free!
What, wouldst thou leave me, Kenelm?
Lilian, you know I love you. I would make
You and my father friends. I'd tell my tale;
And then, if stern to all Macronalds else,
He'd let me call you sister. I'd return
Of my free will. Free! How I envy all things
That no chain binds—birds lessening up the sky,
And winds that sweep on shouting! Would I were hawk,
Or horse, or hound. Ah! would I were the knight—
The stranger knight Sir Oscar! I had borne
His wounds and sickness if, like him restored,
I might to-day ride forth.
He goes to-day?
Knew you not that?
And he goes sound and whole,
Thanks, lady, to your skill; though scarce a month since
Borne to this convent, faint with wounds, he lay
In sorest peril. To your healing hand
And patient care this stranger owes a gift
No less than life.
Sets he not forth at noon?
Was't not at noon?
But say, what keeps you thus so grave and brooding?
Brooding! I, Kenelm?
You.
The lad is right.
Methinks you should be blithe and proud to know
Your patient leaves you cured.
Ay, there's the riddle.
When the knight lay in danger, Lilian's step
Was quick, her eye was bright; but as he grew
In strength, so she in gloom. Her hands are idle
Even as her tongue; see how she plies her needle!
On Monday she began the Greek chief's helmet.
'Tis Thursday now, and there the needle rests
At Monday's point. For some good cause, I trow,
The knight was cured too soon: that chafes her.
Kenelm!
Nay, you're not angry, Lilian?
No, not angry.
I'll prove it further. Yesterday I asked her,
How fares Sir Oscar? Is he well? Whereto
She answered, Well; yes, well; but with a sigh
And look and tone so doleful, you had thought
The man's last hour had come, and not his cure.
Now say, is't not a riddle?
You forget
Yourself, to speak so.
Lilian!
There, all's well.
So! is it thus?
Come, Kenelm, find your bow, I'll see you shoot.
Not now! Mark you yon cloud; there'll be a storm.

div.stage: Sir Oscar and Page pass by window.

lg.l: The knight, Sir Oscar, passes down the walk.
If he should enter, child, still heed my warning—
Let him not know your name or birth.
Why not?
He'd not betray me?
No; not by intent,
He might by chance. Our foes still threat the district;
Wherefore the abbess from the knight has hid
Your name and true estate, and lodged his train
Beyond her walls.
Now speaks he to the page;
Now to the window looks. He will come in.
Then come thou forth with me!
Good faith, not I!
I'd see this knight more closely.
Dost thou heed?
Thou'lt anger me!
Roderick, what wait you for?
To see this wondrous knight, for he's a wizard.
And deals in spells.
Look you, his health restored
Hath wrought her sickness. But I'll stay and foil
His evil charm.

sp.speaker: Lil.

lg.l: Go, Kenelm: heed commands;
I'm not in tune for this.

sp.stage: [Kenelm hurt, and a little indignant, takes up his cap.]

lg.l: Nay, I spoke harshly;
But thou know'st, Kenelm, there are times with all
When no jests please—when one would be alone.
When thou dost bend thy bow, another's shadow
Would spoil thine aim. When thou dost hold thy wrist
For the falcon's perch, another voice would fright
The bird from settling.
Oh, I guessed not that;
If that you mean to draw your bow and aim,
Or lure your falcon down, I'll go; I had gone
Before if I had dreamed thou'dst have me go.
I do not love thee less.
Now, Roderick!
Dear Lilian! mind your aim. Allow for wind;
And shoot not towards the sun. Adieu!
Thou mischief!

div.stage: [They go out by side door.

lg.l: Ah, light of heart!
He comes to say farewell.
What should he else? Strange how one little day
Can change our world! The sun will rise for years
And we wake, toil, feed, sleep, and nothing miss,
Till one day dawns that with it brings a sense
As of a life new-born! No hours gone by
Have known that thrill; no hours to come—nor grief,
Nor joy, nor change—can wake that thrill again!

div.stage: Shortly before this speech concludes Sir Oscar reappears at window, ushered by an elderly man, attired as a servant of the Convent. This attendant, by a gesture, indicates to Sir Oscar to enter the room. Attendant passes on, and disappears. Sir Oscar enters. He wears the dress of a knight of the period, with the exception of the helmet, and wears no plaid, tartan, or any Scottish badge.

sp.speaker: Sir O.
sp.stage: [Whose face shows some slight traces of recent illness, advancing to Lilian.]

lg.l: Deign, dear lady, pardon
For this intrusion. 'Tis a sweet, sad duty
To bid you farewell.
You too much presume
On your new strength; pray sit.
Nay, I'm once more
Myself, ready for tourney or campaign;
And yet, methinks, I'm half ungrateful.
You?
Yes, since the health you gave me back I scarce
Prize at its worth. I think of the dim chamber
In which the sick man lay; of the bright presence
That lit its gloom, and of the gentle hand
Whose touch was balm. At first, in fever's dream,
I thought some heavenly form that stooped to earth
Bent o'er my pillow; and I said with joy
That Heaven was kind; then soon your look and voice
Proclaimed you human, and, with deeper joy,
I said, She lives! she lives! she's of our world!
Then all our world grew fairer.
I beseech you,
You speak not thus of one so little worthy;
Or I may deem my cure but half complete,
And say his fever talks so!
Nay, delirium
Fashions no shape of perfectness like that
I gaze on now. As day by day I grew
In strength, and in the sense of all that's fair,
The more you fill'd that sense. Whene'er you spoke
Or sung, or with your harp beguiled my hours,
Each act revealed your nature. Pardon, therefore,
If less I prize the strength regained that parts us
Than those blest days of weakness when I learned
To know her whom I now must but remember.
To hear such words, yet ne'er again to hear them!
I lack skill
To make due answer and to tell my thoughts;
But wish you may be happy.

div.stage: [She extends her hand to him, which he kisses. The sky grows gradually darker.

sp.speaker: Sir O.

lg.l: So, farewell!
Farewells must come. Forgive me that, being loth
To say the word, I linger; for the eyes
That look their last on joy may well look long.

sp.stage: [Lilian turns aside, gently withdraws her hand, and betrays emotion.

lg.l: Did she in anger turn? not so.
Sweet lady,
You chide not with your lips that I remain;
Does your heart chide me? Would it chide me, dared I
To linger still?

div.stage: [A pause.

lg.l: You have good cause to linger;
The sky grows black with storm.
And is it for that—
For that alone you'd wish me tarry? Ah!
If in an hour hence, in a day, a month,
You could say farewell with no more regret
Than your sweet courtesy gives to all at parting,
Bid me go now; but if the thought presumptuous
That, yet in bud, dares scarce unfold itself
Into a hope, might live; then would I say
This strength you have given back, this frame, this heart—
All that I am is yours; in every pulse,
And nerve, and thought, is yours; and at your feet
Would cast the life which you preserved in vain,
Save your love crown it too!

div.stage: [Throws himself at her feet.

lg.l: I pray you, rise.
Have I too far presumed? Dost bid me go?
I bade thee rise; I did not bid thee go.
And dost not now?
Not if you wish to stay.
Do I but dream of joy? Is it thy will
I stay? Speak! Nay, I ask not words; but reach
Thy hand for sign.
Thou dost! Oh! half I doubt
That Heaven to this harsh world can be so kind
And remake paradise.
Quick to my heart,
And seal this true!
Thou'rt mine!
Ay, thine—thine ever!

div.stage: [Pauses.

lg.l: And we but late were strangers!
Ah! to me
Thou wast no stranger. I had seen thee oft
Ere my eyes met thee.
Seen me!
Know'st thou not
How oft our minds, when earth seems fairest, shape
Some being fit to tread it? Thus at sunset,
When in the lake's pure floor the circling peaks
Beheld their jewelled image, and entranced,
I asked if heaven above or heaven below
Did ravish more with beauty; or in autumn,
When through the woods, sighing with tremulous leaves
Of gold or crimson, like a conscious life
The brook pulsed on, then would I cry, O earth!
How fair thou art! Give me a man to match thee!
In mien let him be noble, brave of heart,
To rule so bright a realm; in war, his voice
Dread as the sea's; in peace, as soft as winds
That roam in summer 'mid the pines, and teach
The dim green twilight tunes. Be such my lord!
And when I met and knew thee first, I felt
That what my heart imagined Heaven had clothed
In mortal form, and that I saw my prayer!
Thy love shames my deserving; yet 'tis true
We loved as in a dream—no thought of self,
No thought of state or fortune. To this hour
I know thee but as lady and as Lilian;
And thou too know'st me but as knight and Oscar.
Yet since the very raiment that love wears
Pleases the eye, tell me in what apparel
Has Fortune dressed thee? What's thy name? thy birth?
Thy serving-men are French, and yet thou speak'st
Our tongue.
My native tongue; I never lost it.
My father, dwelling some brief while in France,
Did choose his bride there, and with her returned
Unto the Scottish glen, where I was born.
I, still a child, my mother's health grew frail,
And, pining much to see her land again,
With me, her youngest born, did she repair
To France, and there amid her kinsmen died.
Those kinsmen loved her child, and one—a noble
Of the French Court—prevailing with my father,
Made me his page. At length, high tales of war
And soldier's fame, recounted by the hearth,
Woke martial longings in me, and I joined
The French king's service; in the which till now
My life has passed. Years since I, sorrowing, learned
My father's death. Now, during war's brief lull,
To Scotland am I come to seek my brother
And mine own people.

div.stage: [Thunder and lightning faintly heard and seen.

lg.l: Well, thy race? thy name?
Knowing what feuds my clansmen wage, and loth
To peril my few followers, I concealed
A name that oft wakes strife. Thou know'st the rest—
That a marauding band, in hope of plunder,
Assailed us; that with spur and sword we forced
Our passage and rode on, till, near this spot,
Faint with my wounds, I reeled, and here was borne,
Blest in what seemed disaster.
Yet not finding
More blessing than you brought.
Thou mak'st my joy
Too full. For this one hour I'll pardon fate
All frowns hereafter. Lov'st thou, what can rob
Oscar Mackane of thee?
Mackane! Of whom
Speak'st thou? Oscar Mackane!
My name, which thou
May'st proudly bear. The son of Fergus I.,
Brother of Murdoch, chief of the Mackanes.
Thou Murdoch's brother!
He still lives?

sp.speaker: Lil.

lg.l: He lives.

sp.stage: [Thunder and lightning somewhat more vivid and audible than before.

lg.l: Would that he ne'er had lived, or thou not sprung
From the same stock!
Wherefore?
In me thou see'st
The child of Angus, late Macronald's chief.

div.stage: [Both rise.

lg.l: Macronald! our hereditary foe!
In fight with the fierce tribe thy brother led
My father fell.
Not by my brother's hand?
Not by his hand,
But by his followers; and, beside the hate
Instinctive towards thy name, that with the stream
Of life we draw even from our mother's breasts,
Know that, where'er I turn, our gaping ranks
Show the fell shafts of thine. My uncles perished
Stemming their onset; my young kinsman David
They snared and slew; that I stand here an orphan
Is due to them, thy kin. Away! a gulf
Between us yawns, and every wave is blood!

sp.speaker: Sir O.

lg.l: Not more thou shrink'st than I. Upon thy breast
That tartan,
unbeheld since childhood, grows
Familiar to me—the abhorreèd emblem
Of a loathed race!

sp.stage: [A short pause, during which he gazes at her, as if bewildered.]

lg.l: Loathed, did I say; and thou
Sprung from that race!

sp.stage: [Thunder and lightning still more vivid and audible.]

lg.l: By heaven, two natures strive
Within my breast! One for my kinsmen's wrongs
Prompts me to hate, the other pleads, Forget
All wrongs for her!
Obey the sterner voice;
For I could deem my father's spirit rose
Frowning that still I listen.
Oscar, go!
I may not love thee, and I cannot hate.
Thou canst not hate! Nor I. If enemy's blood
Flow in thy veins, it flows not in thy soul,
Which has its kin in heaven.
Hence!
Look on me,
As I on thee; I love the thing thou art,
And ask not whence it sprang.

div.stage: [Thunder loud, and lightning vivid.

sp.speaker: Lil.

lg.l: Oh, thou dost strain
My being to its root. I might for thee
Brave living kindred's wrath; but the mute frown
Of the dead who cannot plead, who sleep in trust,
Their child will ne'er be traitor to their blood—
This, this appals me.

sp.stage: [A loud and long crash of thunder and vivid lightning.]

lg.l: Hark! 'tis heaven's own voice
Uttering its prohibition! If thou seest
The fierceness of her struggle whom love tempts
And duty warns; if thou wouldst have me 'scape
My people's curse; by thine own love for me,
Help me; save, save me from myself, and go!
Harsh doom! but I obey thee even in this.

div.stage: [Sir Oscar bends his head low in acquiescence, then slowly retires, and goes out by door opposite to that by which Roderick and Kenelm went out.

sp.speaker: Lil.

lg.l: 'Tis well. I have been true to name and clan.
I have slain my happy youth, and made its grave
An altar to my race. To-morrow's sun
Will fall where we two stood; on us together
Will fall no more. And he, alas! will not
My doom be his? Duty! Had I no duty
To him who taught me first what life might be,
With love's strong arm broke for my sake the chain
Of deadliest hate? No more to hear the voice
That woke my heart to life, to bear within
This ceaseless yearning widowhood of soul
For him who lives, but lives no more for me!

sp.stage: [The sound of a horn is heard.

lg.l: That horn! his train set forth!

sp.stage: [The Squire and Page and other followers of Sir Oscar pass at back.]

lg.l: They pass! Even now
The gates are opening!
Oscar, Oscar, stay!
By all I bear, I know what thou must bear.
I might have doomed myself to appease my race,
Not thee, not thee! Oscar, canst thou forgive,
Canst thou accept this heart, which, for thy sake,
Bursts all the chains of hate, tradition, clan?

sp.speaker: Sir O.
sp.stage: [Advancing, and extending his arms towards her.]

lg.l: Thou art my clan, my fate, my all in all!

div.stage: [She throws herself into his arms.

div.head: [SCENE I.]
div.stage: Scene.—Noonday. A valley in the Highlands. A wood of oaks at back. Mountains in the distance. On one side an arched gateway, leading to an old tower. Rude rustic benches, with the massive felled trunk of an oak, are scattered about. An old rough stone of some size, which serves for goal in the race, is seen on side of stage opposite to gateway. As the curtain rises, it discovers the clansmen of the Clan Mackane, with other men and women of various ages, including children of both sexes from the neighbouring glen and village. Michael and Colin, as near connections of the chief, wear each an eagle's feather in his bonnet. Other Clansmen wear each in his bonnet a sprig of holly, as the badge of the Mackane. As the curtain rises, shouts from some of “Allan! Allan!” From others of “Dougal! Dougal! Dougal!” All are looking off scene towards side at back.

lg.l: Allan!
Dougal!
Allan!

div.stage: Allan enters, running rapidly towards the stone, the goal, amidst the applause of the greater part of spectators, who exclaim, “Well sped, Allan! Allan!” Dougal enters almost instantly after Allan, and runs after him to the goal.

lg.l: Take heart, good Dougal! He need nothing boast;
You'll beat him yet. You're the chief's thirteenth cousin,
And, by my reckoning, he is but the twentieth.
Indeed you ran him hard.
A minute more
I'd past him—see, he pants, while I—I'm fresh
And sound of wind—scarce breathed!

div.stage: [They laugh.

lg.l: Ay, ay, we know,
But that some sorry chance still plays you false,
You'd always be his master.
Am his master.
Jest on. You're jealous that I danced with Rose.
My next dance is with Allan.
Let him take
My cast-off gear and wear it.
Your cast gear!
Braggart!
Braggart!

div.stage: [They lay their hands on their sword-hilts.

lg.l: No strife! What! strife to-day,
When, till our scouts report the foe, we hold
High festival to welcome the return
Of Oscar, and our chief's brother, long deemed dead
Hear you?
Take hands!

div.stage: [Dougal and Allan somewhat sulkily shake hands.

lg.l: Be the time henceforth spent
In Oscar's honour.

div.stage: [All but Michael and Colin disperse themselves over the ground. Some converse in groups standing, sitting, or reclining on the grass. Others examine the hammers which have been brought back. Others take up bows and arrows and prepare to shoot. Clansmen who went out return and join the rest.

sp.speaker: Mic.
sp.stage: [To Colin, who has remained with him in front.]

lg.l: But 'tis strange he comes not,
To share these sports with which our people greet him.
Oscar? He's still with Murdoch.
'Tis not wise
In Murdoch to delay him.
You forget;
Murdoch's your chief.
No more the chief he was.
Since that dark hour when by Macronald's band
His son, young Kenelm, was borne off and slain,
But one thought holds him, and his fitful will
Scarce brooks restraint of reason. Even here,
Where we have marched from home, that in this glen,
Our thinned force may the better cope with Cameron—
Here on Macronald's borders has he spurned
His offered peace, and challenged double strife,
Though weak to meet it single.
He's your chief.
And leads us to our ruin.
He's my chief;
I'll follow him to ruin.
Follow madness?
If madness be his humour, 'tis his choice,
Not mine. He's still my chief.
Silence! he comes—
He and his brother Oscar.

div.stage: Enter Murdoch and Oscar from archway. Followed by Sir Oscar's squire and page, they advance to front, Sir Oscar still wearing his dress of 2d Act, and no Scottish plaid, tartan, or badge. The various groups come to front to meet them. The squire and page mix with the Clansmen and others, and converse. Murdoch stands a minute silent and absorbed, then sits abstracted on felled trunk of tree.

lg.l: Kinsmen, friends,
Pardon if I, a seeming laggard, come
To thank your welcome of me, who went forth
A child, and am returned to you a man.
Beseech you make not my delay offence,
For I was held in counsel with my brother
On what concerns us all.
Thrice welcome, Oscar,
The brother of our chief!
Ay, long live Oscar!
A welcome for the chief too; long live Murdoch!

div.stage: [Waving his bonnet.

sp.speaker: Some Clanspeople.
sp.stage: [With a fainter cry, in which the rest do not join.]

lg.l: Ay, long live Murdoch!
Cold greeting for their chief!
They greet you, brother.
I say your people greet you.
Greet me? Thank them. Say that I thank them.

div.stage: [Relapses into gloomy reverie.

lg.l: To the full, we both
Exchange our love with you—your chief and I.
But let your sports proceed. Here on the strath
Let each man draw his bow, and he whose shaft
In three encounters strikes the nearest home,
Shall for his trophy wear a jewelled sword,
Which from my foe in deadly fight I plucked,
Warring for France!
A costly prize!
Put forth
Your best skill to deserve it.
Ay! ay!
Brother, you
Will witness this contention?
I? not now.
I have no humour for't.
Affairs of weight
Engage my brother still. Some later hour—
Say two hours past the noon—shall you contest,
And he award, the prize.
Even now our meal
Lies spread on yonder slope. Follow! To Oscar,
So late restored, we'll drain our cups.
Ay, full ones!
You from the glen and village will partake
Our feast. Sweet, by your leave.

div.stage: [To Effie, who proudly takes his arm.

lg.l: By my leave, Michael.
By yours when she is yours.
Come, Rose!
Too late!
I promised him the next dance.

div.stage: [Going up with Allan.

lg.l: So!

sp.speaker: Mic.
sp.stage: [Looking back on them as he is about to go out.]

lg.l: Remember,
No strife, 'tis Oscar's day; a health to Oscar!
Ay, ay, we'll all drink that.
A cup to Oscar!

div.stage: [All Clanspeople and others, Murdoch, Oscar, and Colin excepted, rush out gaily, the men with their partners; the squire and page amongst the rest.

sp.speaker: Sir O.
sp.stage: [To Murdoch, who still sits in gloomy abstraction Colin reclining near him on the grass.]

lg.l: Murdoch, their feast lacks its best grace, if you,
Our chieftain, hold aloof. With me, and join them!
Join them in what? their mirth?
Their chief should make
Their mirth his own.
'Tis well; you lesson me,
My new-found brother.
And your younger brother
By some ten years, I grant; I'd not offend.

div.stage: [Going.

sp.speaker: Mur.

lg.l: Nay, Oscar, go not. If the wide earth hold
Aught dear to me—the which I doubt—'tis thou.

sp.stage: [Looking earnestly at Oscar, then speaking to Colin, and laying his hand on Colin's arm.

lg.l: Mark you not in his look a something—something
That hints the face we miss?
Our Kenelm's face?
Peace! Did I bid thee name him?
Speak not!

div.stage: [He again falls into deep and gloomy abstraction.

sp.speaker: Sir O.
sp.stage: [Seating himself on a bench by Colin, and speaking to him apart.]

lg.l: Pray you,
What cause has moved him thus?

sp.speaker: Col.

lg.l: Sir, 'tis a wound
That I did ill in probing. See! again
He's lost!
His mood is on him. When it falls,
He shuns all converse, breaks not fast, nor gives
His nights to sleep, but sits in moveless gloom.
And yet, I have at times the luck or skill
To rouse him and dispel his evil hour.
I will essay it. Mark! I speak to you.

sp.stage: [Then addressing Sir Oscar in louder tone, that Murdoch may hear.

lg.l: If you demand of me what deeds in fight
Your brother wrought, my task is hard to choose
What I shall note, or where begin. The growth
Upon his chin was down, not hair, when first
He drew claymore. When was it—when—say, chief,
When first blood dyed your steel?

sp.speaker: Sir O.
sp.stage: [Who, with Colin, turns and observes Murdoch.]

lg.l: He heeds you not.
When, when?
Was't not that far-off night
(What years have flown since then—'twas early spring—)
When our brave lads drove off the foeman's herds,
And we, belated, followed far behind?
See'st thou that night?
He's rapt; you squander breath.
That night of misty moonlight, when, like dogs
That track the boar, they with deep-chested yell
Strained on our path?
Now mark!
You rouse him not.
Who were they that pursued
With yells and opening jaws? The accursed Macronalds!

sp.speaker: Mur.
sp.stage: [Suddenly kindling into interest, and grasping Colin's arm.]

lg.l: Ay, the Macronalds! Colin, thou say'st well.
Go on; what did I then? what then?
Thou knowest.
Some five, whose speed outstripped the rest, o'ertook
And hemmed us round. Then stood we twain at bay.
At bay, and, like the boar you spoke of, rent them
With tusks of steel. A living wall they stood;
We smote, and like a shattered wall they fell!
Thy axe made breaches there!
The more part sank
Beneath your arm.
Thou say'st so!
At great odds
Did you contend!
And he, young hawk, first struck
His quarry there! You had been proud to wear
His tartan later on Glen Allan's field.
Thrice at the Glen's mouth, with a shout that mocked
The ocean's roar, the fierce Macronald beat,
While with a scanty force your brother thrice,
Rock-like, repelled them—
Till 'twas turn of tide,
And the roar sank, and all that sullen sea,
Moaning, ebbed out, nor left a trace behind
But the white surf of dead! Among their dead—
Ay, ay; say on; say on!

div.stage: [To Colin.

lg.l: Among their dead,
Three of Macronald's race—their bonnets bore
The eagle's plume—lay stretched.
I had dealt on them!
I, only I!
Thou only, chief.
Ha, ha!
Thy words are wine, brave heart! As I had known
Their ruthless tribe should one day from his lair
Hunt my poor whelp to death, I took revenge
Beforehand; but my heart, unslaked, could drink
Revenge as sand drinks water. I am parched
More rain! more rain!
He's roused at last.
By hatred
To Lilian's race!
That you have borne dire wrongs
I may not doubt. Still prudence, not revenge,
Should sway a leader. If I hear aright,
The Camerons, counting on your wasted strengths,
Are now no less Macronald's foes than yours.
Against this new foe should you turn your swords
Forgetting former feud.

sp.speaker: Mur.

lg.l: Forget our debt
To the Macronald? I'd as soon forget
My mother's last kiss, or my dead wife's first,
Or my slain boy's parting clasp. To him and his
We owe our shorn strength, ravaged land, crushed pride—
Fuel enough for hate. But if in you
It smoulders, I'll throw oil on.

sp.stage: [Motions Sir Oscar to trunk of felled tree, while Colin makes a deprecating gesture. Murdoch and Sir Oscar sit. A short pause.]

lg.l: You came back
This morn as from the dead, and yet I smiled not.
You have seen my face light up—as the scarred cliff
Beneath the storm-flash—while a laugh more bitter
Than groans broke from me; but you have not seen—
You will not see me smile.
My brother!
Yet
I once could smile, and, strange! for joy could weep,
I had a boy, in whose soft brow, clear eyes,
And trick of speech his mother lived again.
And often when he spoke a sudden echo
Surprised me from the ruins of my youth;
And when he trod the health my fancy leaped
The years to come, and saw the eagle's plume
Stream from his bonnet, as, with drawn claymore,
And our wild war-cry on his lips, he led
Our van to battle, as a comet leads
The trail of light behind it!
Ay; he ne'er
Had shamed his stock, chief!
Well, this boy, my Kenelm,
Who was to me—guess what an only son,
His mother in the grave, is to a father!—
Going forth to fight, I left him in the care
Of humble folk, whose lowly roof I deemed
Would be a safe and less suspected shelter
Than my own walls; but there the hunters tracked him,
Seized, bore him off, and doubtless dyed their hands
In a child's blood. My Kenelm!
Ask you still
Why for one hope I live, and only one,
Revenge upon his murderers?
My heart, brother,
Bleeds at this deed abhorred. Not less than you
Would I pursue the doer.
Sir, I thank you;
I had so much believed.
But could Macronald,
Or kin of his, be privy to such horror?
No, 'twas some caitiff follower!

sp.speaker: Mur.

lg.l: You can weigh this!
You're nice in right! What hunted creature asks
Of the pursuing throng whose spear transfixed it?
It turns and rends the foremost. Save you, sir,
I was a father, and your temperate virtue
Offends my too rash blood. Farewell, just brother!

sp.stage: [Going, he turns to Colin, who is following him, and waves him back.

lg.l: Not now, I'd be alone.

div.stage: [Murdoch goes out by gateway into tower.

lg.l: When he shall learn
That to Macronald's child I stand betrothed,
What bounds will curb his fury?
Look you, sir,
The chief went hence in anger; you do ill
To cross his mood.
How if his mood go wrong?
Your part is still submission. If I bid
My dog to leap a chasm, though the plunge
Be death, he takes it. What your chief has willed
Is your will; or it should be.
And it might be,
Were I his dog.

div.stage: Enter Michael hastily.

lg.l: Kinsmen, I bear grave news.
Those we sent forth have learned by sure report
That Cameron, whose advance we deemed was near,
Falls back towards England.
England!
Whence by bribes
And pledge of Scottish spoil he gains allies.
Thus reinforced, he bends his swollen strength
At once against Macronald's clan and ours.
Then but one choice is left, to sell life dearly.
Were it not wisdom if, with your old foes,
You now made league 'gainst new ones?
League! no league
With the Macronalds!
Others say not so.
Know you not then that three days since their chief,
Young Malcolm, proffered peace and his alliance
Unto your brother?
Was this so?
Albeit,
Old rancours in our breasts at first prevailed,
To both clans had this union been safety,
To ours existence. That we were most rash
To spurn it, hour by hour grows clear to all.
Then it was spurned?
Almost before 'twas utter'd.
By Murdoch, who with scorn drove back the envoy.
All this admits of cure. Murdoch, a Scotsman,
No less than chief and clansman, when he hears
That Cameron fees English swords against us,
Will join with Malcolm!
Will he so? 'Tis fit
He learn your scheme betimes.

div.stage: [He goes out by gateway towards tower.

lg.l: I'll seek my brother.
How takes Macronald this?
Even as befits
A name we hate but honour. He prepares
To leave his castle, and pursuing Cameron,
Engage him ere by English succour joined.
Would Murdoch did the like.

div.stage: [Going.

sp.speaker: Mic.

lg.l: 'Twere well.

sp.stage: [A shout without of “A dance! A dance!” Some of the Clanspeople are here seen entering at back, and motioning to the rest.

lg.l: But see our people,
Now from the feast press in for song and dance.
Stay for their sport; so shall you win their love!
Sir, I am theirs. 'Tis thus they show me welcome.

div.stage: [Other Clanspeople re-enter, accompanied by men, women, and children from the neighbourhood, also Sir Oscar's knight and page. The two latter take seats to witness the dance. Foremost Clansmen, with cries of “Clear, clear the ground!” remove off the stage the trunk of felled tree, benches, &c. Others shout, “A song, a song!”

lg.l: Their mirth well pleases me. These hearts so light
In danger's front are just the hearts to face it.
Sir knight, your speech smacks of the song we dance to.
Fair maid, let's hear that song.

div.stage: [All approach their partners except Sir Oscar and Michael, who sit at side in front, and Sir Oscar's knight and page, who sit at back. Pipers, dressed as clansmen like the rest, enter with bagpipes, also a harper with harp, and other musicians. Dougal advances to Effie, who, after coquettish hesitating glances at Allan, takes Dougal. Allan advances to Rose, who, after similar glances at Dougal, takes Allan. Song sung to music, in which the notes of the bagpipes are distinctly heard.

[Before the dance is resumed, Sir Oscar advances to Effie; Michael advances to Rose; Effie withdraws her hand from Dougal, and gives it to Sir Oscar; Rose withdraws her hand from Allan, and gives it to Michael. For a moment Dougal and Allan turn away sulkily; then each seizes the disengaged hand of his former partner. Sir Oscar's squire and page now each take the disengaged hand of a female dancer. The dance is resumed, the dancers again repeating the last four lines as chorus, and using their plaids as before. When the dance has reached a certain point, scene closes.

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: A rude hall in the tower. Early afternoon.
Enter from inner door Murdoch and Colin.

lg.l: How say'st thou? He would have me league with Malcolm!
In friendship clasp the hand our blood has stained,
Forego the sole sweet joy that life has left.
A retribution matchless as my wrongs!
Such is your brother's purpose.
But he comes,
Doubtless to speak it.

div.stage: Enter Sir Oscar from without, through open door.

lg.l: Tell me what's thy name?
You brought me seeming proof you were my brother.
'Twas false; if through your veins my blood did course,
You could not be at heart so alien.
Has Colin slandered you, or dare you tell me—
Me, chief of the Mackanes—you counsel friendship
With Malcolm of Macronald?
Strife in brothers—
If they must strive—brooks no observer's eye;
I'll answer you alone.
Go, Colin.

div.stage: [Colin goes out.

lg.l: Yes, 'tis true;
I counsel union.
Bold, even in a brother!
You grant your followers, worn by feuds, too weak
Singly to cope with Cameron; yet your force,
With Malcolm's joined, might brave him. You'll not doubt
What course befits you when you hear that Cameron
Leads English mercenaries 'gainst you both,
And, with the spoil from bleeding Scotland wrung,
Pays hireling stabbers! Murdoch, you'll protect
Scotland—our mother!
Kenelm was my son.
Much I love Scotland, more I hate Macronald.
You stand here chief and leader. With your honours
Accept your duties. When the time admits
Of private vengeance, then be only Murdoch;
But now, when clan and country call on you,
Be Scotsman, chief, and gentleman.
And cry
To Malcolm, I repent, I sue for aid!
You give as well as sue, if, following him,
You march towards England on the foe.
Has Malcolm
Set forth towards England?
So our tidings run.

sp.speaker: Mur.
sp.stage: [Musingly to himself, but heard by Sir Oscar.]

lg.l: Then his main force goes with him, and his castle
Defenceless lies. We're near it, on his borders!
What mean you?

sp.speaker: Mur.
sp.stage: [Still to himself, but still heard by Sir Oscar.]

lg.l: Yet he has nor wife nor child;
No crevice in his armour where the shaft
Envenomed might pierce home; he mocks my vengeance.
Had Angus lived, he was a father; he
Had felt the pangs I bear.
If a child's cry
Could reach him, 'mid the fiends', and startle hell
With a new torment! He has left a daughter.
Last night, 'tis said, she to Macronald's home
Returned—now dwells there!
Ay, we're on his borders!
Hold, Murdoch;
What dost thou plan?
You rouse me from a dream.
Methought I played a game, and rose no winner;
But still with equal fortune, child for child!
Speak! what's your thought? Heaven grant my fears have wronged you.
Plott'st thou against the freedom or the life
Of Lilian of Macronald?
Ha! you're quick
To solve a riddle, brother.

div.stage: [Laying his hand on Sir Oscar's shoulder.

lg.l: Take thy hand
From my stained person, and unteach thy lips
That name of brother. If thou practise ill
On her, or by connivance suffer it,
Then look not to Macronald's line or Cameron's
For thy worst enemy, but find him here,
In me who own thy name and share thy blood,
But scarce forgive my mother that thou sprang'st
From the same womb that bore me!
Does my sense
Serve or delude me? Do I hear or see?
Thou beard'st me!
Go! the fire is in the cloud,
But bursts not yet. To shelter, boy; to shelter!
What is the daughter of my rival's house
To thee—a stranger?
Stranger is she none,
To her I, sick and wounded, owed my life;
To her the love that crowns life. Know in her
My late preserver, and my wife betrothed!
Betrothed! Thou! she!
I much suspect my thoughts
Of wandering.
Say it, if thou canst, again;
Thou wedd'st with a Macronald?
Not more sure
That yon sun shines than, if we live, we wed.
Thy words smite on my brain, as on a door
Foemen with sword-hilts knock in time of war,
While those within, half-drowned in sleep, rise staggering,
And let in murder! To my wakening sense
So dost thou stand. False, not to me alone,
But to thy sires and clan; false to the dead
And to the living; false to tomb and altar;
To nature's instinct false, as if life's stream
Within the veins should roll back on the heart
That was its source, and choke it! False as—nay,
Thou'rt not this thing; say I but charge on thee
My fancy's monstrous growth; say thou'rt my brother,
And crush not him who called thy father, father!

div.stage: [Throws himself in supplication at Sir Oscar's feet.

lg.l: I pity thee.
Ay, thou wert ruthless else;
But dost thou yield? Thou dost!
I cannot yield
When only fury pleads.

div.stage: [Turning from him. While Sir Oscar speaks these last words, enter Michael, Colin, and several other Clansmen.

lg.l: Murdoch, these tidings
Should lead to prompt resolve.
Then meet that fury!
Words have no power to blast, be this my tongue.

div.stage: [Rushes with sword on Sir Oscar, who seizes his arm, wrests sword from him, and throws it aside. Colin takes it up.

lg.l: His sword drawn on a brother!

div.stage: [All but Colin look menacingly at Murdoch.

lg.l: In brief madness,
Which cooler thought rebukes.

sp.speaker: Col.
sp.stage: [Reaching Murdoch his sword, and speaking significantly apart to him.]

lg.l: Though all else frown,
I'm still thy hand to do the thing thou bidd'st.
You say well, Oscar.
All here's storm and darkness.
If ever light break in, I'll better pay
The dues I owe you, brother!
Lead me forth,
I'm feeble, and want rest.

div.stage: [He goes out, leaning on Colin, who, as he goes out, turns and regards the rest with a look of fierce reproach.

lg.l: Oscar, our hope
Is fixed on you. He whom his frenzy rules
No more rules us.
No more, no more!
To counsel then, for all
Await your voice.
In what befits a brother
You shall command me. He is still my brother.

div.stage: [All go out by open door, opposite to that by which Murdoch and Colin went out.

div.head: SCENE III.
div.stage: Sun fast declining; about an hour from sunset. An upper apartment of Malcolm's Castle. A door at side. Two large painted windows at back. Between them a narrow door (open), which commands a Gothic terrace, and gives a glimpse of a lake beyond. Another door at side. Three or four portraits of former Macronald chiefs, in their Highland and clan costume, on the walls; amongst these, conspicuous to audience, is a portrait of Lilian's father, Angus. Another portrait opposite side-door conceals a sliding panel. An oratory, with altar and plain crucifix, surmounted by a small lamp, not lighted in this scene, is also conspicuous to audience. Old armour, swords, shields, battle-axes, &c., grouped on walls.
Enter Lilian, still dressed in slight mourning, and Roderick.

lg.l: What say'st thou, Roderick? The clan Mackane
Are on our frontier!
Ay; from where they muster
They see our battlements. We from the convent
Returning, barely missed them. By heaven's grace
You're now 'neath Malcolm's roof; at home once more.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.stage: [Involuntarily referring to Sir Oscar, and overheard by Roderick.]

lg.l: Then is he near?
Who? Malcolm! Well, you know
He with his followers pursues the Camerons.
He has left you thinly guarded; but fear not.

sp.speaker: Lil.

lg.l: What sound was that?

sp.stage: [The panel slides open. Kenelm enters. Closes the panel, and advances. Lilian. Sportively.]

lg.l: Ah, mischief! art thou here?
Why by that panel enter like a thief,
When all else use the door?
Because I choose
To do what others do not, and I love
Things curious and forbidden.
Then Dame Nature
Errend in thy sex; thou shouldst have been a woman.

sp.speaker: Ken.

lg.l: Alas, I'm not a woman! Yesterday,
Descending by the secret stair whereto
That panel leads, I strove to thread the maze
Of winding vaults below; I'd torch in hand,
But lost my way. Now had I been a woman,
I'd found my way, for women are like cats:
They see best in the night, and are at home
In all that's dark and crooked.
'Tis so, Lilian!
'Twas she that taught me first the panel's trick.
To-day I'd better luck; kept straight my path
Through the oozing walls of stone, till mounting steps
Upbore me to a grate, which, pushed, gave way,
And I was in the sunlight—none to watch—

sp.stage: [With a sudden change to bitter sadness.

lg.l: As free as when I trod my father's hills!
Lilian, I tell you, I will see my father;
Not all my love for you can stop the hunger
For home that gnaws me.
My poor Kenelm!
Boy!
Must you again be warned? Remember well
The vain attempt at flight might prove your death.
Poor petted fawn! keep in thy lady's bower,
And thou art safe.
Chide not! 'tis nature's self
Prompts his desire. Kenelm, though you must bear
This durance, still you know that Lilian's heart
Would beat even with your joy if you were free.
And yet she'd miss thee much.
I do believe
You would have all free as you are—hold none captive—
Except some wounded knight too early cured.
Well, wounded birds, uncaged, will oft fly back,
And so may he.

div.stage: [Lilian turns from him rather sadly.

sp.speaker: Rod.

lg.l: Peace! peace!

sp.stage: [A horn is heard without, followed by the tramp of a horse.]

lg.l: A horn! And now
The tramp of horse! Perchance 'tis news of Malcolm.
Perchance a foeman's summons. The Mackanes,
You say, are near?

div.stage: [Kenelm, who is listening, slightly starts, then conceals his emotion.

lg.l: But humbled, and too weak
To brave your cousin's wrath.
How! The Mackanes
Are near—my father near!
'Tis now the hour
When Randolph comes back with his hawks. I'll meet him,
And ask him of his sport.
And to the hall
Will I, and find what stirs. 'Tis nought, dear lady,
To cause you fear: I will report full soon.
Come, lad!
A moment.
Lilian, if now
Or ever I have angered you—and oft
I've given you cause for anger—you'll forgive me?
The madcap always loved you.
Ne'er did Lilian
Doubt that, dear boy.
Heaven's blessing rest on thee!
Enough, enough! This sugar spoils the teeth.
Come, come, pet fawn!
Say rather prisoned fawn.
There's much to give and take, boy; the pet fawn
Is tethered and shut up; but the wild fawn—
Is free—is happy!
Humph! he's shot and roasted.

div.stage: [Roderick and Kenelm go out by side door.

lg.l: Dear, hapless boy! His name was on my lips
When Oscar left me. I had almost said,
Your nephew lives! Well that I checked my tongue!
That knowledge then had led to new assaults
From Murdoch, which resisted, in the strife
The lad perchance had fallen! For his safety
I must be secret still; but when a bride
I fly to Oscar, he shall share my flight.
'Twill crown anew the royal hour we wed,
To say, Thy brother's son by me preserved!
Ah me! when comes that hour? Is all a dream?
Did he indeed lie wounded at St Catherine's?
Did I there tend him! And oh! did we part
But three days since? He promised on the third
To send a trusted friar, by whose report
I should our time and place of meeting learn.
The sun declines, and yet he has not sent.
She is within, alone?

div.stage: Re-enter Roderick, followed by Sir Oscar, who still wears no plaid or other tartan, or any badge of the Mackanes.

lg.l: So please you, lady,
The stranger knight.

div.stage: [Goes out.

lg.l: Thou, Oscar!
My heart's heart!

div.stage: [They embrace.

lg.l: Thou'rt here indeed; but in this house, in peril!
No peril, love. None here surmise my birth.
I'm but a stranger and a knight from France,
By you befriended. No, sweet Lilian,
'Tis you who are in peril. In this fortress,
Feebly defended, you but court attack,
While enemies, if few, yet subtle, plot
Against your freedom—life. Hear me, who know
Your danger, and in you would save myself.
Ere dawns to-morrow's sun, give me such right
As none else have to guard you. Be my wife!
Thy wife to-night!
To-night.—I, with my train,
Will come and bear thee forth. A league from hence
A wayside chapel stands. There shall the priest
Await us; and, the rite performed, I'll lead thee
To the safe shelter of his sister's roof,
Where thou shalt bide till I returning claim thee.
This night! Doubt not my love, but in that step
A girl takes passing from old life to new—
There's awe as well as joy! Grant time.
Thy danger
Of time admits not. Further know, my brother,
For gravest reasons, stands awhile deposed
From his command, and by the more part I
Am named his deputy. At break of day
I lead our clansmen to the aid of yours,
Who singly strive with Cameron.
Your Mackanes—
They league with us—with Malcolm!
You shall learn
Hereafter how this fell; now hold it true.
May this blest union ever bind you friends.
Heaven grant it, sweet; but to my suit. Once more
I say thou art in peril. Ere I don
A soldier's harness, let me bear thee hence
To a sure refuge. If thou still dost fear
These hurried nuptials, I obey thy will
And leave thee there unwed. But if—

sp.speaker: Lil.

lg.l: Stay, Oscar:
Thou goest to battle. He who gives the victory
Alone foreknows the end. I shrink no more.
Be it so. Ere thou goest, join our fates—
Claim me for thine!

sp.stage: [Extending both her hands, which he takes.]

lg.l: Then, com'st thou back a victor,
This swelling heart shall hail thee all my own;
And if—
If fate be darkest?
Ay, even then
I should be blest, for I should join thee soon.
Till then, oh! dearer far thy memory
Than any hope surviving. I should know
That for some blessèd hours I called thee mine.
And, cleaving to that thought, look grief in the face
And say, I once was his! Take, take me, Oscar!

div.stage: [She falls on his neck.

lg.l: Perfect in trust as goodness! At thy word
I take thee. See, the sun goes down apace;
Ere it has set two hours, I will return.

div.stage: [They turn towards door, which is open. Murdoch, disguised in the travelling garb of a minstrel, looks in at door. He wears a cloak with a hood, which partially conceals his face and quite disguises his identity.

lg.l: Ah, look! who's he that on us bends a gaze
So strange and fixed?

sp.speaker: Sir O.

lg.l: Some pilgrim, by his garb.
Why dost thou start?

sp.stage: [Advancing to door, and speaking to Murdoch, who is retiring.

lg.l: Who art thou? What's thine errand?

sp.speaker: Mur.
sp.stage: [Who assumes the gait, manner, and voice of an aged man, returns.]

lg.l: A travelling minstrel I, who, on my way,
Have tidings for this house.
Shall he approach?
His news may be of import.
Ay, but go not.
Enter.
You, fellow, bear his harp.

div.stage: Enter Murdoch followed by Evan, bearing harp. Evan, who is one of Macronald's domestics, wears the Macronald plaid.

lg.l: Fair lady,
See I in you the daughter of the chief?
Of him who was the chief—my father's dead.
'Tis she.
These woful words must I repay
With sounds as harsh. As minstrel late I served
The young Monteith. Your father loved him well.
A rival of my lord in maiden's love
Slew him in strife o'er wine. These news I bear
To Monteith's distant kinsman, and was bid,
When journeying to him, to acquaint Macronald
With our dire grief.
My father was the friend
Of the brave house you serve. I, as his child,
Lament its loss.
Lady, a hapless house!
A century since, its head, in heat of youth,
Espoused the daughter of his enemy;
Since when the wrathful hand of heaven has pressed
Upon his line who broke the holy laws
Of pact and race. All that were heirs to him
Have come to ends untimely.
Strange! his tale
Sounds like a warning.
Can this move thee?

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.stage: [In a low tone apart to him.]

lg.l: No.
Thou art my fate. Whate'er betide, thou'rt mine.

div.stage: [Oscar bends to her, and whispers reassuringly.

sp.speaker: Mur.

lg.l: Ay, whisper, whisper! Let your amorous lips
Grow glued even in my sight.

sp.stage: [Aloud, as Lilian and Sir Oscar turn to him.]

lg.l: My errand told,
I of your goodness, lady, would entreat
Short rest and shelter. Then I take my way.
Take freely all you need; I ask not now
That you should prove your skill upon the harp,
Your journey's solace, doubtless. Ere you go
I may demand a lay.
Whate'er you ask,
I am obedient. If the lay be harsh
And the strings jar and crash, bethink I'm old,
And my hand lacks its cunning.
Else I'd win
Such music from the chords, the strain should dwell
On your charmed ear till life itself lapsed with it.
I take your will for deed. Your name?
'Tis Uric.
Evan, conduct the minstrel to his chamber.
May food and rest refresh you.
I'm your debtor.

div.stage: [Evan, bearing Murdoch's harp, goes to door. Murdoch slowly follows him.

lg.l: Time speeds, and bids me haste; remember, sweet,
Two hours past sunset I return.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.stage: [Observing Murdoch, who at door turns and gazes on her intently.]

lg.l: Again
That fixed, mysterious gaze!

div.stage: [Murdoch follows Evan out by side door.

lg.l: What dost thou fear?
Is't strange that minstrels' eyes, alive to beauty,
Should feed on thine?
'Twas folly, and 'tis past.
Then for brief while farewell.
When next I come
'Twill be to claim in thee a joy so sure
Nought can unbase it, and so absolute
It cannot know increase!

div.stage: [Going.

lg.l: Thy voice, dear lord,
Doth speak for both our hearts. Till night farewell.

div.stage: [Sir Oscar goes out by side door. Lilian gazes after him.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.stage: [Returning from door, and sinking into chair.]

lg.l: The hour is fixed, the hour that seals my bliss;
Yet bliss is solemn, and my heart lies hushed
Like earth before the dawn. Strange, joy should wear
A look that chills me. I could almost deem
Again yon minstrel's gaze, that, like a cloud
Enfolding thunder, veiled what still it showed,
Bent, moveless on me. Lilian, shame! art thou
The child of Angus?
Angus!
From the wall
His darkening mien upbraids me, that I blend
His foeman's blood with his. I'm fancy's sport.

sp.stage: [She again gazes on the portrait of Angus, her father, which gradually fades away, and changes slowly to the spectre of Graham's wraith, which is precisely the same in appearance, expression, and attitude as when seen in first act. Lilian continues to speak while this change takes place.]

lg.l: And yet a horror broods in all the air,
Some spell still holds my sight. Ha! now it fades,
The pictured semblance fades; and now puts on
Some ghastly change! No more my father, there
It stands—again the vengeful spirit stands
That warns our house of danger. Is it death
That now impends?
Stern phantom, when before
Thou cam'st in thy mute terror, I was firm,
Firm even to death! but now I love and fear.
If in thine awful, unconjectured home
Old thoughts of human love can reach thee still,
Claim me not yet; have pity!

div.stage: Enter Kenelm by open door at back, cap in hand.

sp.speaker: Ken.

lg.l: One last look!
She knows not 'tis the last.

sp.stage: [Aloud, perceiving Lilian, rushing to her, and placing his arm round her.]

lg.l: Why Lilian!—

div.stage: [As Kenelm rushes to Lilian, the spectre of Graham's wraith suddenly vanishes from the frame, in which the portrait of her father Angus resumes its place.

lg.l: 'Tis gone!

div.stage: [She reclines almost fainting in Kenelm's arms.

div.head: Scene
div.stage: Scene.—Same as last scene of last act. Night. A lighted torch on each side of mantelpiece. The lamp suspended over the altar-piece is also now lighted. Door at back closed. Vivid moonlight seen through windows; some clouds, however, are also visible. The scene discovers Lilian seated and Margery. Lilian wears a tartan scarf of the Macronald pattern over a white dress, the skirt of which is long for riding. Margery is engaged in placing a rose in Lilian's dress.

lg.l: Thanks, thanks, dear Margery; you have laid out
My riding-cloak—your own too?

div.stage: [Pointing to riding-cloaks and head-dresses laid near.
Enter Roderick from side door. His face wears a look of anxiety.

lg.l: Madam, all
Lie here prepared.
'Tis well; when once our summons
Comes, it will ask despatch. We must ride far
Ere midnight, Margery.
Ride far to-night?
Forgive me, lady, but this sudden humour
Holds not with reason.
Have I not possessed you
Already of the cause? The knight, Sir Oscar,
Has learned that danger threats me.
Humph! 'Tis well
To guard you from your foes, but who shall guard you
Against your guarders? How shall I answer Malcolm,
That you, at stranger's bidding, quit his walls?
How answer Malcolm? With my heart's dear thanks
For past protection. He's my friend and cousin;
No parent to command me.
He's your chief
And guardian of your honour.
Not so, Roderick.
I'm guardian of my honour. Malcolm lives
His proper life. 'Tis well; but I live mine.
These matters are beyond me. I but know
Our chiefs by their own arms protect their women,
Nor leave that care for strangers. I must tell
Sir Oscar that Macronald's walls best guard
Macronald's child, and that you stir not hence.
Roderick, you'll ne'er say that.
Shall I be plain?
'Tis love, not danger, prompts you to this folly.
Ride you not to your bridal?
If it were so?
What say'st thou?
If it were so, says my lady—
If she did ride to church, why 'tis a journey
That most maids of her age are apt to take,
And one I plan myself—what then?
What then?
Then should I act and speak.

sp.speaker: Lil.

lg.l: Like Lilian's friend,

sp.stage: [Motioning him to sit, which he does. She bends over his chair.

lg.l: Who from her childhood made her whim his law.
What did I ask and you not grant? To ride?
You led my palfrey. Would I hawk? 'twas you
Who trained my falcon; and you oft would laugh
Because I wept in sudden penitence
To see the heron struck. Or would I sail?
'Twas you who, smiling on me from the helm,
Held in the veering sheet; and will you now,
Old playmate—now I venture all life's freight
Upon the deep, and take the voyage whose end
Is Eden or a quicksand—now I love—
Will you now first be froward to your Lilian?
My duty, girl!
Thy duty is to love
And help the child who loves thee. Would she 'scape
To happiness, 'tis thou shouldst aid her flight—
Raise bars, not fix them; and thou wilt! Dear Roderick,
Thou shalt go with me and thy grandchild here—
This very night stand by me at the altar,
That I may feel the hand that led my father
When he was yet a child, in my joy's hour
Rest on my head and bless me. Say thou'lt go!
Strive not with women: 'gainst them man's resolve
Is straw, his sternness wax. Ay, what thou wilt.
Thou art old Angus' daughter. To the last
I'll follow where thou lead'st, and bless my fate
That I, in extreme age, have lived to see
Love's crown upon thy youth.
Nought shall divide us.
My home be henceforth thine. But we must haste
Our preparations. Where is Kenelm; seek him,
For he must with us.
Kenelm! You have touched
On what disquiets me; though now 'tis night,
He still is absent; where, with whom, unknown.
I've strictly questioned; none within have seen him
Since fall of sun.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.stage: [With an effort to disguise her anxiety.]

lg.l: Why, then, he has gone forth
With Donald to the herd, or else prevailed
Upon our oarsmen to put out and row
In the clear moonlight.
Ah, how fair a scene!

div.stage: [She watches from window.

lg.l: Your look is grave; the boy's safe?
Would I knew it.
I've fears for him. The scarf and cap he wore,
As I but now have learned, were found by Donald
Some half league from the Castle. Do these signs
Augur no deed of violence? You know
The hate that some here bear him, and how swift
A death might reach him did he purpose flight.
You'll keep this from my lady.
Ay, 'twere ill
At such a time to grieve her, unless proof
Confirm the doubt; and yet my heart is heavy
For the quick step that comes not.

sp.speaker: Lil.
sp.stage: [Returning from window, which she closes if open.]

lg.l: On the lake
Or on the shore he must have wandered far;
Or else—how think'st thou, Roderick?—his great yearning
For home and kindred has at length o'erpowered him,
And he has fled. When last we met, his arm
Clasped me in such a long and fond embrace
As now seems like a farewell. If it were so,
Heaven's love preserve him!
Thrice amen to that;
But I've an errand by this chance delayed:
'Tis from the minstrel who to-night arrived,
And soon goes hence—well that he should—a stern,
Unsocial, silent man, whom none will miss.
I thought him what you say; but oft we err.
He doubtless mourns his chief untimely slain,
And we have ta'en for sternness in his mood
What was but sorrow. Well, what is this errand?
Ere leaving he would see you—pay his thanks.
He has a suit too—some most private suit,
Meant for your ear. So much he importuned,
That I have let you know this.
Poor and old,
'Tis like he has such need as pride unbares
Only to few.
Say that I'll see the minstrel,
That I await him here.
Retire; and, Roderick,
Press instant search for Kenelm.
I'll not fail.
